source.title: The Interpolation Phase Transition in Neural Networks: Memorization and Generalization under Lazy Training

record.file_problem: Full text is present. The paper studies two-layer neural tangent models and lazy training, rather than standard deep networks trained with stochastic gradient methods.
record.tranche_reason: The paper theoretically tests whether a specified two-layer neural tangent model can interpolate arbitrary labels, and includes a numerical train-error illustration. Its architecture, data model, and optimization procedure differ from the claim's standard deep-network SGD settings.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the stated arbitrary-label interpolation result and the numerical train-error result. The paper does not report experiments on completely random labels, test error at chance under random labels, unstructured inputs, label-noise fractions, explicit regularization effects, or learning order. The Adam experiment in Appendix A fits a linear target and reports generalization error, not random-label fitting.
record.test_reason: The paper proves interpolation capacity for linearized two-layer neural tangent models and conditional convergence for specially initialized two-layer networks. These results do not establish random-label fitting by standard deep networks using stochastic gradient training with unchanged hyperparameters. Its numerical training-error result uses structured regression targets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. More precisely, the authors prove arbitrary-response interpolation for sufficiently overparameterized NT models and characterize their test error through equivalence to infinite-width kernel regression and polynomial ridge regression with self-induced regularization. Extension to gradient-trained nonlinear networks requires specific initialization, smoothness, width, and scaling conditions; controlled or good test error is conditional on the target and data regime.
record.recipe_differences: The main analysis uses a two-layer neural tangent linearized model with random fixed first-layer weights and minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolation, under isotropic spherical covariates. Section 5 gives a theoretical connection to gradient-flow training under a specific symmetric initialization. This differs from standard deep-network SGD experiments on image data.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpolation results depend on the overparameterization threshold N d/(log(N d))^C ≥ n and the specified spherical covariate and weight distributions. The test-error characterization requires additional sample-size and activation assumptions.

fits_no_version.finding: Corollary 3.1 proves full row rank and exact interpolation of arbitrary responses with high probability under its activation, spherical-data, sample-size, and overparameterization assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sufficiently overparameterized two-layer NT models can interpolate arbitrary responses on high-dimensional spherical covariates.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 reports that minimum-norm NT regression training error vanishes sharply as Nd/n crosses 1 for a structured target with additive Gaussian noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-norm NT regression exhibits an interpolation threshold near one parameter per sample in the tested synthetic regression setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 5.1 establishes exponential convergence of gradient flow for a two-layer network with fixed output weights, symmetric initialization, smooth activations, and specified width and scaling conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Specially initialized two-layer networks can converge to interpolation under sufficient lazy-training conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Proposition 3.1 bounds fitting independent random binary labels with positive margin in norm-constrained two-layer networks by a capacity of order Nd log(Ld/δ). It does not evaluate a training algorithm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorization of random binary labels at positive margin requires sufficient parameter capacity in norm-constrained two-layer networks.

record.problems: The evidence for random-label fitting is theoretical and indirect: no random-label experiment is reported. The numerical train-error experiment uses a structured target, d = 20, and only 10 repetitions. The connection to actual neural-network training is conditional on specific initialization and lazy-training assumptions; the paper notes those sufficient conditions are not expected to be sharp.
record.rows_left_out: No results qualifying as separate claim-related rows were identified. Appendix A's two-layer Adam experiment uses a linear target and reports generalization error, not the random-label fitting behavior.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting by standard deep networks trained with stochastic gradient methods, unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters, and chance test performance.
Training-time comparison between real and random labels and convergence as the corrupted-label fraction increases.
Zero training error on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs using the same networks.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test performance across fractions of randomly corrupted labels.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels during training.

record.verdict_notes: The NT model's fixed random weights define tangent features; its fitted coefficients represent linearized first-layer changes, rather than ordinary second-layer-only training. Neither theoretical capacity nor the structured-target illustration warrants a V1 support verdict. Gaussian covariates in the capacity bound do not establish V3's same-network unstructured-input fitting behavior.

versions.untested_parts: Tests arbitrary responses in a theoretical two-layer NT model and reports one train-error illustration with structured labels; does not report completely random labels, test error at chance, or standard deep networks trained with stochastic gradient methods.

rows.subject: NT model (1)
rows.stage_stated: neural tangent regime; first-layer weights fixed and coefficients a fitted
rows.operation_detail: Minimum ℓ2-norm interpolation of arbitrary responses on isotropic spherical covariates; interpolation existence is proved when N d/(log(N d))^C ≥ n.

conditions.value: c0 d ≤ n ≤ d^{1/c0} with polynomial relation to d

rows.measure: Existence of an exact interpolator for arbitrary responses
rows.value: rank(Φ) = n with high probability; an NT interpolator exists with high probability for any choice of responses when N d/(log(N d))^C ≥ n
rows.note: This is a theoretical result for a two-layer NT model with a restricted spherical data distribution, not an empirical random-label test of standard deep networks or SGD.
rows.check: The full-rank result is correct, but exact interpolation capacity in an NT model does not measure V1's training behavior in standard deep networks. The condition must also include Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, including the sample-size windows and activation requirements; polynomially related n and d alone is insufficient.

rows.subject: min-ℓ2 norm NT regression
rows.stage_stated: neural tangent model; fitted by min-ℓ2 norm regression
rows.operation_detail: Fit data generated from a structured target plus Gaussian noise; report training error across network parameter count and sample size.
rows.value: train error vanishes sharply as N d/n crosses 1
rows.uncertainty: Results are averaged over nrep = 10 repetitions
rows.locator: Section 2.1, Figure 1 description and accompanying text
rows.note: Labels are structured, not random; the textual description gives no exact train-error values. Random labels are therefore not directly tested by this result.
rows.check: The reported vanishing training error is correctly described, but the labels come from a structured polynomial target plus Gaussian noise. Minimum-norm NT regression on these targets does not test completely random labeling or any other listed version. Remove this as a claim-related result row.
